questions.first: I regret not studying harder at school.
questions.explanation: 'Wish + subject + had + past participle' expresses regret about a past action.

questions.first: They are building a new stadium in the city centre.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive ('is being + past participle') is used because the action is in progress now and the agent is not important.

questions.first: 'I will finish the report by Friday,' Tom told his manager.
questions.after: he would finish the report by Friday.
questions.explanation: Reported speech backshifts 'will' to 'would'; 'that' after 'told his manager' is optional.

questions.first: Nobody in the class is as tall as Peter.
questions.explanation: The superlative 'the tallest' is used to compare one person with everyone else in a group.

questions.first: It isn't necessary for you to finish the report today.
questions.explanation: 'Don't need to'/'need not' are semi-modal/modal forms meaning there is no obligation to do something.

questions.first: Could you look after my cat while I'm away?
questions.explanation: 'Would you mind + verb-ing' is a polite way of making a request; 'look after' becomes 'looking after'.

questions.first: If you don't leave now, you will miss the train.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if...not', so 'if you don't leave' becomes 'unless you leave', keeping the same future meaning.

questions.first: Tom is less experienced than his colleague Sarah.
questions.explanation: 'Less...than' can be rephrased as a negative equal comparison: 'not as...as'.

questions.first: 'Where did you put the keys?' she asked me.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order, not inversion; 'wanted to know' reports the question, and 'did...put' backshifts to 'had put'.

questions.first: People say that this painting is worth millions.
questions.explanation: 'People say that + clause' can be rephrased with the passive pattern 'subject + is said + to-infinitive'.

questions.first: Could you please reduce the volume of the TV?
questions.explanation: 'Turn down' is a phrasal verb meaning to reduce the volume or level of something; both 'of' and 'on' are used before the device.

questions.first: It was a mistake for him to sell his old car.
questions.explanation: 'Shouldn't have + past participle' criticises a past action, showing it happened but was the wrong decision.

questions.first: The committee will announce the results next week.
questions.explanation: The future passive ('will be + past participle') is used because the focus is on the results, not on who announces them.

questions.first: Despite the rain, the match continued.
questions.explanation: 'Even though' introduces a concession followed by a full clause, unlike 'despite', which needs a noun or '-ing' form.

questions.first: I last saw my cousin in 2019.
questions.explanation: The present perfect with 'since' plus a specific point in time expresses how long it has been.

questions.first: It's possible that the flight will be delayed because of the storm.
questions.explanation: 'Might be' expresses possibility, matching the meaning of 'it's possible that'.

questions.first: Nobody plays the piano as well as Clara in our school.
questions.explanation: The superlative 'the best' is used because Clara is better than everyone else in the group.

questions.first: People believe the painting was stolen during the war.
questions.after: to have been stolen during the war.
questions.explanation: 'Is believed to have been' is the passive reporting structure used to rephrase 'people believe that...'.

questions.first: I'm sure she left her umbrella at the office.
questions.explanation: 'Must have + past participle' expresses a confident deduction about the past.

questions.first: This year's festival was not as successful as last year's.
questions.explanation: 'Less...than' is the direct equivalent of a negative 'as...as' comparison of degree.

questions.first: The teacher let the students leave early because of the heat.
questions.after: leave early because of the heat.
questions.explanation: 'Were allowed to' is the passive form used to rephrase 'let someone do something'.

questions.first: 'I didn't take your pen,' Mark told me.
questions.explanation: 'Deny + verb-ing' reports someone saying they did not do something.

questions.first: If I were you, I would accept the job offer.
questions.explanation: 'My advice would be to...' is a common alternative way of giving the advice expressed by a second conditional.

questions.first: They've increased the price of petrol again.
questions.explanation: 'Has risen' (present perfect of the intransitive verb 'rise') describes the result of the price going up again.
